At approximately 11:00 a.m. on December 18, 2020, an employee was training other
employees during the implementation of EPIC (a new electronic records charting
system). The employee was working with employees who were treating COVID-19
positive patients.  The employee contracted the virus and died from COVID-19 as
a result from the virus SARS-CoV-2.
At 8:20 a.m. on November 19, 2020, Employee #1, employed by a construction
company, was installing the last piece of plywood subfloor on the second-floor
deck of a single-family home. While working, the employee slipped on a patch of
ice and slid under the guardrail, falling 20 feet to the compacted soil. The
employee sustained a broken bone in his back and broken ribs due to the impact
of the fall. The employee was hospitalized for treatment.
At 1:29 p.m. on December 17, 2020, Employee #1 was positioned at the top of an
aggregate belt conveyor, preparing to overfill bins for the following day's
operations. While using a shovel to remove aggregate buildup, Employee #1's arm
became caught between the belt and the belt roller. Emergency services were
called, and Employee #1 was transported to the hospital, where he was treated
for injuries to his arm. The employee was hospitalized.
At 12:30 p.m. on December 10, 2020, Employee #1, employed by a construction
company, was working on the second floor of a townhome unit, installing a door
light on the outside facade. While leaning out of the second-floor sliding glass
door, the employee lost balance and fell 13 feet to the compacted soil. The
employee sustained broken ribs and internal injuries. Emergency services were
called, and the employee was transported to the hospital for treatment and
hospitalization.
At approximately 1:53 p.m. on December 20, 2020,  the fire chief and department
personnel attended a coworker's funeral on November 23, 2020, and on November
26, 2020, the department responded to a fire call.  Within the span of five
days, five employees tested positive for COVID-19. The employee acquired
COVID-19. The employee died on December 20, 2020, and death was attributed to
was caused by COVID-19 with superimposed bacterial pneumonia.
An employee, a patient care technician, was performing duties which involved
contact with patients including bed baths, phlebotomy, assistance with toilet
and obtaining of vital signs. The employee was exposed to patients who later
tested positive for COVID-19. The employee contracted COVID-19 and died April 7,
At 11:00 a.m. on December 4, 2020, an employee was working for an urban county
agency that regulated and administered transportation programs. He operated
heavy equipment. In this instance, he was operating a front-end loader or front
end loader. He was maneuvering the front end loader along a graded wall. He was
bringing leaves up to the top of a ramp to pour leaves from the front end
loader's bucket into a dump truck. The right wheels of the loader were climbing
the ramp, while the left wheels were on a lower grade below the ramp. The center
of balance on the loader shifted, and the loader overturned on its left side.
Memorial for 2 to 2 1/2 days, where his burns were treated with creams and a
bandage. No surgery was required. Employee #1 was released from Torrance
Memorial on June 11, 2020.
At 11:45 p.m. on December 8, 2020, two employees were operating a press while
putting 24/24 steel into a die and cycling the machine. One employee used the
two-hand controls to cycle the press, while the other employee had his hands in
the nip point at the same time. As a result, both employees sustained crushing
injuries to their thumbs and possibly their index fingers.  The employee was
hospitalized.
An employee was working as a mechanic or automotive technician for a new car
dealer. His work schedule was 7:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. from Saturday to Tuesday
and Friday to Sunday. He worked in the service department. Two workers there
tested positive on January 8, 2021, and one more worker tested positive on
January 9, 2021. The employee's last day of work was January 15, 2021. On that
day, he was experiencing symptoms of COVID-19. The following day, January 16,
2021, he took himself to the hospital. He was tested positive for COVID-19, and
he was hospitalized on that day. He notified his employer of his hospitalization
at 5:00 p.m. on January 19, 2021. On January 19, 2021, his employer contacted
the Division to report that three of its workers had tested positive for
COVID-19, and that one of these three, the employee, had been hospitalized. On
January 22, 2021, the Division opened an investigation with the employer.
At 12:30 p.m. on October 13, 2020, Employee #1 was operating a silage truck.
Once the truck was loaded, Employee #1 proceeded to exit the corn field.
Employee #1 made a right turn on the edge of the field, and he felt like the
rear tire slid and the truck veered towards the driver side.  Employee #1 tried
to correct the truck, but it overturned. Employee #1 suffered a dislocated left
shoulder and was hospitalized.
At 6:30 a.m. on January 20, 2021, an employee, a gardener, attempted to change
the blade height of a mower while the blade was moving. The employee's
fingertips on the left hand were amputated by the blade.  The employee was
hospitalized.
At 11:45 a.m. on January 19, 2021, an employee operating a melt furnace and
molten metal erupted, hitting a metal door. The eruption caused second-degree
burns to the employee's head and shoulder, as well as a bone fracture. The
molten metal's impact led to significant injury, requiring hospitalization for
confronted by two individuals (a man and a woman) trying to rob him. The
employee had his own gun and shot the male, killing him. The woman then shot the
employee in the chest, killing him.
On January 18, 2021, a maintenance employee who worked for a dairy foods company
died from COVID-19. The employee had tested positive before his death. The date,
time and other details leading up to exposure are not indicated in the
narrative. Information regarding engineering, administrative and personal
protective equipment controls for COVID-19 are also not included in the
narrative.
At 12:15 p.m. on November 3, 2020, an employee was operating a motor vehicle on
a highway when the employee was struck head-on by another motor vehicle
attempting to pass a pickup truck. The employee was transported by air to a
local hospital where the employee died from multiple blunt force trauma
injuries.
At 10:00 a.m. on February 4, 2021, an employee secured, a length of string
around two four by four boards. At some point, the employee slipped and fell
through and unguarded opening in the walkway into a weir. The employee was then
pulled into a one thousand foot long pipe and killed by drowning.
At 8:00 p.m. on October 15, 2020, Employee #1 was working with the 3141 Flexo
Machine. Employee #1 needed to remove scrap materials from the drive side of the
machine. Employee #1 reached into the machine, past a 20-inch wide conveyor belt
that was still in motion. The machine had not been shut down. Employee #1's hand
was caught by the conveyor belt, pinching her finger. Paramedics were called so
Employee #1 could receive treatment for the laceration to her finger.  Employee
#1 was treated without hospitalization.
At 10:00 a.m. on September 23, 2020, while grouting column foundations, two
steelworkers dropped a 4x12-foot rectangular section of Robinson decking. The
decking fell to the ground and struck Employee #1. The employee sustained
serious unspecified injuries and was hospitalized for more than 24 hours.
Two employees were working in a nursing home. Employee #1 worked in the kitchen
of the home and was in self-quarantine for three days before requiring
hospitalization for a COVID-19 infection. Employee #2 was on scheduled leave for
seventeen days prior to her hospitalization but had performed her direct patient
care duties prior to her leave. Both employees became ill and had difficulty
breathing and went to the emergency room on their own. Both employees were found
to have COVID-19 while in the hospital but both recovered from their illnesses.
At 3:30 p.m. on January 23, 2021, an employee was working as a dispatch manager
for a local general freight trucking company. A truck driver had been assigned
to transport a pre-loaded 51 foot (15.5 meter) trailer that was staged in the
lot. The truck driver could not connect the truck's wiring harness to the
trailer, because the electrical socket on the trailer was broken. The truck
driver made a phone call and sent a photo of the damaged plug to the office,
located at an adjacent lot. The dispatch manager left the office and drove his
personal vehicle over to the trailer. He flagged down the driver of a jockey
truck that was driving in the area and spoke him. The dispatch manager asked the
driver if he could assist him to make sure the electrical connection was
working, and the driver agreed to do so. The driver of the jockey truck made his
maneuver and backed up toward the trailer. According to the driver, he was
reversing slowly, checking his left and right mirrors, and looking through the
truck's rear window while lining up and reversing. The driver indicated that he
was unaware that the dispatch manager was positioned between the trailer and his
truck while it was in reverse. As the jockey truck driver continued to back up,
the dispatch manager was pinned and crushed between the rear of the jockey truck
and the trailer. He was hospitalized. He died from his injuries.
At 7:30 p.m. on January 27, 2021, Employee #1 was attempting to load a pallet
into a truck trailer using an electric pallet jack. While maneuvering the pallet
jack, the employee lost control and pinned his right foot between the electric
pallet jack and a pole located in front of the trailer. The employee sustained a
fractured right foot and was hospitalized for treatment.
At 3:30 p.m. on January 4, 2021, an employee performed overhand bricklaying on
an exterior wall working from a fabricated frame scaffold. At some point, the
employee fell approximately twenty-five feet through the exterior wall and
killed by multiple, unspecified contusions, abrasions, and fractures.
At 11:15 a.m. on February 2, 2021, an employee was working for a firm that made
ready-mix concrete. He drove concrete mixer trucks. He had parked his truck, and
he was walking from it across the yard to the dispatch office to give the
personnel there his paperwork. He was not wearing high-visibility clothing. On
the way to the dispatch office, he passed in front of another concrete mixing
truck that was pulling into the yard. The driver of that truck did not see the
employee. The driver pulled forward and struck the employee. The employee was
killed.
At 5:00 p.m. on February 4, 2021, an employee was working for a firm that
manufactured fabricated structural metal. He was performing abrasive blasting
with steel shot. He was wearing a supplied air respirator (SAR). While using the
supplied air hood, he lost consciousness. A pressure testing operation
downstream on the plant air line allowed nitrogen to backfill into the
compressed air line. This test introduced an asphyxiant into the system. The
employee was killed.
At 11:21 a.m. on January 30, 2021, an employee was working for a landscaping
company. The employer was an individual who was a sole proprietor. He was not an
arborist or professional tree cutter. He took on odd jobs and hired friends he
knew and paid them in cash. The employer had been hired by a homeowner to remove
multiple trees located at a private residence. The employer brought along his
friend, the employee to help him remove approximately 36 trees. This was their
second day on the worksite, as they worked there on the previous weekend as
well. The Employer had paid the employee in cash the week prior for his work and
planned to do the same for the work performed on the weekend of this incident.
The employer was cutting down one of the trees from the bottom with a chainsaw.
The employee and a coworker were holding a rope that was tied around the top of
the tree. They were doing this to guide the tree was it fell. According to the
employer and the police report, when the tree began to fall, the coworker ran
out of the way of the tree. The employee, though, somehow did not move out of
the way or actually ran into the tree. He received fatal head trauma injuries.
He was was taken to a hospital, where he was pronounced dead. According to the
employer, the employee had not been provided with and was not wearing any type
of head protection, such as a hard hat.
At approximately 10:20 a.m. on February 4, 2021, the investigation involves a
teacher and four teaching assistants who shared an otherwise empty class -
teaching being conducted remotely over the internet. The teacher was located in
the center of the classroom and was COVID-19 negative and without symptoms. The
symptoms included a cough, congestion, and fatigue. She tested positive for
COVID-19 on January 20, 2021. Two days later, at 10:00 a.m. on January 22, 2021,
she was hospitalized.
At 2:30 p.m. on January 27, 2021, an employee was on top of a crane trolley
guiding wire rope onto the hoist drum. The employee and his coworkers were
conducting conventional reeving of a new hoisting wire rope. The process
required the employees to loop a cable around the drum and then lower it to the
bottom block and back to the drum several times while adjusting the cables with
an equalizer. During this process, the employee became caught in the drive shaft
of the crane trolley and was killed.
An employee was working as a teller for a commercial bank. She contracted
COVID-19 and was hospitalized.  At 11:00 p.m. on January 25, 2021, she died.
On Monday, January 25, 2021, an employee was working for a firm that sold and
mounted tires. The employee was mounting an agricultural use tire on a forklift
used at a dairy. Another worker at the firm provided a tire that was 16 in. (406
mm) in diameter. The rim on the forklift was 16.5 in. (419 mm) in diameter.
After the employee had mounted the tire on the rim, he started filling it with
air. He was using a clip-on air chuck. He was filling the tire to approximately
25 to 35 psi (172 to 241 kPa). The tire was on the floor. A coworker watching
the activity instructed the employee to disconnect the clip-on air chuck. As the
employee reached for the valve stem, the tire disintegrated. The employee
suffered fractures to his left arm and wrist. He was hospitalized.
At 1:00 p.m. on June 3, 2020, the truck center supervisor dispatched the
operator to deliver three boat motors/transmission to a customer. The motors
were transported in a 53-foot trailer. The standing floor of the trailer was
approximately 46 inches in height from the horizontal ground. The operator
delivered the motors to the destination customer and parked the truck-trailer
combination on level flooring near the docking yard of the trailer unloading and
loading complex. The operator was pulling something on the trailer floor toward
the opened trailer back door.  The operator was ejected out of the trailer,
hitting his head on the ground.  The operator was hospitalized to treat a
traumatic head injury, a left wrist fracture, a concussion, and multiple
lacerations.
An employee was working as a cashier at a supermarket or grocery store. She was
working in a checkout aisle. There was a large acrylic plastic, such as
Plexiglas, barrier between her and any customers. She was wearing a face
covering, and customers she was interacting with wore face coverings as well. At
8:04 a.m. on January 4, 2021, she began her shift. At approximately 10:00 a.m.
she was sent home due to pain caused by an abscessed tooth. Two coworkers helped
her sit down, because she had not taken her diabetes medication that morning.
They were within 1.8 meters (6 feet) of the employee while providing this
assistance, but only for a short duration, less than 15 minutes total. This was
the last day the employee reported to work until January 21, 2021. On January 6,
2021, the employee experienced an elevated temperature and cough. The next
morning, January 7, 2021, she went to a regional hospital and took a COVID-19
test. The result was positive. At approximately 10:00 a.m. on January 7, 2021,
she was hospitalized. She was given Remdesivir, Dexamethasone, and antibiotics.
She was released the following morning. The Division was notified by the
employer of her hospitalization at approximately 2:13 p.m. on January 7, 2021.
The Division arrived at the facility on January 28, 2021. Upon arrival, the
Division initiated an opening conference with the assistant manager, human
resources manager, company supervisor, and the employee, who was the union
representative. The employee was not aware of a particular exposure incident
which resulted in her illness. She believed it must have been at work, because
she did not have any other potential exposure. She stated that her employer
enforced physical distancing and face coverings at the workplace and went "above
and beyond" when addressing COVID-19 hazards. The employee's husband developed
COVID-19 symptoms on January 6, 2020, the same day as the employee.
At 1:07 p.m. on August 26, 2020, Employee #1 was engaged in passing materials
from inside a building to a scaffold through a window opening.  Employee #1
stepped through the opening.  The 2 by 4 wood blocking the access fell.
Employee #1 fell approximately 6 to 8 feet into the building. Employee #1
suffered back pain and was treated without hospitalization.
At approximately 12:00 p.m. on January 25, 2021, an employee may have been
infected while working a second nursing job. The employee died from
complications from a COVID-19 infection.
At 2:30 p.m. on January 25, 2021, Employee #1, employed by a construction
company, was using a table saw to rip a wood board at a commercial building
site.  The employee was pushing the board with his left hand.  When he reached
to turn the power switch off with his right hand, the board kicked back, and his
left hand was pulled into the blade.  One finger was amputated by the saw, and
two other fingers lacerated.  The employee was transported to the hospital and
admitted for treatment.  A physician treated the amputation and needed to
surgically amputate the two severely lacerated fingers.
At 6:00 a.m. on December 29, 2020, Employee #1 was climbing the ladder on the
back of the delivery truck, slipped and fell to the ground injuring his head.
The employee was then taken to the hospital and admitted for treatment.
On Monday, January 25, 2021, an employee was working for a city fire department.
He was a fire fighter. At approximately 5:40 p.m., a commercial structure fire
at an athletic shoe store was reported to the fire department. The employee was
dispatched on the response. The fire had begun on the roof of the building. The
store's employees used handheld fire extinguishers to exit the building and
called 911, emergency services. The fire spread to the second floor. The fire
fighter employee was working on the interior of the structure. He was wearing
the required PPE and SCBA to shield himself from burn and inhalation hazards.
High winds from outside the structure led to a rapid increase in the fire's
intensity. At 6:15 p.m., the employee suffered second-degree burns to his upper
back. He was hospitalized. The employer, the fire department, had provided
training and ensured that the fire fighters were current in their training. The
department's fire fighters were wearing the personal protective clothing
required under Article 10.1 of Group 2 in Title 8 California Code of
Regulations.
At 10:13 a.m. on January 28, 2021, three maintenance employees were in a freezer
room troubleshooting improperly frozen cooked chicken parts discharging from the
liquid nitrogen Messer Immersion and Spiral Freezer. The immersion freezer and
the internal freezer tub were designed to contain a bath of liquid nitrogen to
flash freeze the chicken. One of the maintenance employees, who was
troubleshooting the freezer, used a tool to bend the bottom of the stainless
steel bubbler system dip tube upward inside the tub of the immersion freezer.
The bubbler system was part of the liquid control system that maintained the
level of liquid nitrogen in the immersion freezer tub. Soon after the freezer
was restarted, liquid nitrogen in the immersion freezer tub overflowed onto the
floor due to the damaged dip tube. The liquid nitrogen that spilled out of the
freezer converted to vapor due to the changes in temperature and pressure and
displaced oxygen from the air. The three maintenance employees succumbed to the
oxygen deficient atmosphere inside the freezer room. The plant superintendent, a
maintenance employee, and a quality control technician went to the freezer room
and attempted to help the employees when they also died due to the oxygen
deficient atmosphere.
At 5:30 a.m. on January 10, 2020, an employee, a fire fighter, responded to a
structure fire and was raising a 35-foot extension ladder when his gloved hand
was caught in the extending section. The employee suffered a partial fingertip
amputation of the right ring finger. The injured employee was treated and
released from a local medical center.
On January 8, 2021, an employee was power washing a turkey barn using a power
washer attached to a power takeoff device (PTO) powered by a tractor. The
employee had finished washing the barn and was likely winterizing the pump by
adding antifreeze when the incident occurred. In order to add antifreeze to the
machine on his bended knee and hands on the floor. According to the coworker, he
was proactive to help in the process since this was his regular job as
maintenance. He grabbed the nitrogen tank from the shop on a hand truck which
was not secured. The moment he stopped at the location of the machine where the
injured employee was working, the unsecured nitrogen cylinder tank fell and
amputated the left-hand ring finger and middle finger of the injured employee.
The injured employee suffered amputation on his ring and middle fingers. He was
treated at Santa Rosa Memorial Hospital. The employee was hospitalized for four
days. The cause of the accident was an unsecured nitrogen tank that fell onto
the injured employee's hand.
An employee was working as a driver for an automobile dealership and was tasked
with driving new and used cars to the dealer. The employee began to feel sick
and went home and then to the emergency room. The employee was diagnosed with
COVID-19 and was hospitalized for six months. The employee eventually died due
to COVID 19 at 5:00 p.m. on December 7, 2020.
An employee was working on a water canal.  The employee's last day of work was
installing the windows. At some point, the coworker left the platform, crawling
into a window to work while the employee stayed on the platform. The telehandler
sat on an incline and at some point after the coworker left the platform, the
unsecured platform overturned and the employee fell approximately six feet. The
employee received severe head trauma and was killed.
At 11:00 a.m. on January 15, 2021, an Employee #1 and Employee #2 were
performing cleanup operations in an abandoned building alongside 8 coworkers.
Employee #1 and Employee #2 were in an abandoned elevator shaft pit trying to
free the legs of a metal shelf that became caught on the wall of the building as
it was being removed. The metal shelf was being removed with a skid-steer loader
attached to a chain and hook which was being carried on a ramp. The ramp crossed
over the elevator shaft pit acting as a bridge to the outside of the building
leading to a dumpster. As Employee #1 and Employee #2 tried to reposition the
metal shelf it began to lean towards the west side of the ramp toward the
elevator shaft pit. Two large vertical unsecured platforms (which were assumed
to be walls)  that contained packing material and floors for future elevator
cars sat inside the elevator shaft pit. None of the employees knew the large
platforms were unsecured.  Concerned that the metal shelf may fall into the pit,
Coworker #1, Coworker #2 and Coworker #3 climbed onto the one of the platforms
using a long metal bar for leverage in assisting the removing the large metal
shelf.  When they applied pressure on the platform, the platforms fell on both
Employee #1 and Employee #2, crushing Employee #1 and killing him and injuring
Employee #2. Employee #1 and Employee #2 were struck by two falling platforms,
packing material and floors that fell into the pit. Employee #2 was treated and
released at a local hospital.
Employee were working in a skilled nursing facility when a COVID-19 outbreak
occurred. Two of the employees contracted COVID-19 and subsequently required
hospitalization for treatment of their infections. Three additional employees
contracted COVID-19 but did not require hospitalization for treatment of their
infections.
At 1:45 p.m. on January 8, 2021, Employee #1, employed in a manufacturing
facility, was working on the conveyor assembly and adjusting the tracking of the
conveyor. While the conveyor was operating, the employee attempted to move the
belt. When the employee's hand made contact with the belt, his arm was pulled
into the conveyor. The injury resulted in a fracture. Emergency services were
called, and the employee was transported to the hospital for admission and
treatment.
At 8:00 a.m. on November 30, 2024, an employee working as an automobile mechanic
was attempting to fill a tire with compressed air. The side wall of the tire
ruptured directing compressed air at the employee's mid-section. The employee
was hospitalized to treat internal injuries, including damage to his small
intestine requiring surgical repair.
At 12:00 p.m. on January 7, 2021, Employee #1, employed by a manufacturing
company, was operating a paper plate machine in a production facility. While the
machine was running, Employee #1 reached into the point of operation and his
right hand was struck by the moving parts of the machine. The incident resulted
in the amputation of the tips of two fingers on his right hand. Emergency
services transported the employee to the hospital, where he was treated and
admitted for his injuries.
At approximately 12:00 p.m. on September 20, 2020, an employee was working on
four smoke detectors inside a cinema auditorium. The employee was using a
21-foot Little Giant Type 1A ladder. The employee fell from a Little Giant Type
1A ladder. The employee received a traumatic brain injury as a result of the
fall. The employee died from these injuries.
At 3:20 p.m. on January 11, 2021, an employee was attempting to move a trailer
stuck in the snow with a spotter vehicle, using a bucket loader.  While pulling
the spotter and trailer with a bucket loader, the chain snapped, coming back
into the cab of the loader, striking the employee in the head. The employee was
hospitalized to treat a laceration and bleeding on the forehead, a brain bleed,
and a forehead skull crack.
At 1:30 p.m. on November 4, 2024, Employee #1, a supervisor, was climbing into
the back of a pickup truck from a Tommy lift gate to collect equipment. Employee
#1 stepped onto the lift gate and then onto the truck bed, but while upset with
other employees for improperly storing equipment, his foot became caught in the
cross member of the gate, causing him to lose balance and fall backwards. During
the fall, his foot remained caught, and he struck his head on the ground.
Employee #1 lost consciousness for approximately 3 minutes before emergency
medical services arrived. The employee was hospitalized and treated for a
concussion.
At 12:20 a.m. on January 7, 2021, Employee #1, a driver employed by a logistics
company, was loading product onto a trailer using rolltainers at a warehouse
dock. While Employee #1 was on the ground near the trailer, another driver
hooked up to the trailer and pulled it away from the dock. Employee #1 was
trailer which had all the doors and windows closed. The employee died from
carbon monoxide poisoning and methamphetamine use.
At 11:45 a.m. on January 21, 2021, Employee #1 was working on the roof of a
two-story residential building.  He was installing an ice and water shield when
he slipped and fell, a fall height of 20 feet, and impacted the frozen ground.
The employee was transported to the hospital and admitted for treatment of a
fractured leg.
Employee #1, a 60-year-old male, was feeling ill for two weeks (between August 5
and August 19, 2020). He experienced headaches, blurred vision, disorientation,
and dizziness. He felt his illness was due to extreme heat. He reported his
illness to his supervisor at 12:00 p.m. on August 19, 2020. His supervisor told
him to leave early and take the rest of the day off.  Employee #1 was sent home
and advised to use sick leave. After he went home, he experienced a headache and
blurred vision. Employee #1 went to Kaiser Urgent Care the next day for
evaluation.  This employee's symptoms support a heat-related illness. The doctor
diagnosed the employee with heat exhaustion (primary), blurred vision, and
headache.  He was treated without hospitalization.
At 1:55 p.m. on November 20, 2020, an employee was cutting sheet metal. The
employee put the sheet metal on the Wysong metal shear, when his gloves slid
across the sheet metal toward the metal shear blade. When his hand slid across
the sheet, the employee went to catch himself and his foot slipped, pressing the
bar to engage the machine. The Wysong shear cut the tip of two of his fingers
off.  The employee was treated without hospitalization.
An employee was working in a hospital and was working with a coworker who had
flu symptoms and later tested positive for COVID-19. The employee contracted
COVID-19 and was hospitalized on December 21, 2020. The employee successfully
recovered from her infection.
At 3:00 p.m. on January 20, 2021, an employee was operating a 'walkie stacker'
pallet jack.  The employee had just passed through the garage door. The employee
had begun closing the garage door, while he was still traveling through the
opening with the pallet jack. The employee was then walking backwards, looking
up at the garage door while it was closing. The employee's foot became caught
under the leading edge of the pallet jack, and he fell backwards with his foot
pinned under the jack. The emergency brake stopped the pallet jack as soon as
the employee released the handle, but his foot was already under the pallet
jack. Two toes on the left foot required stitches. There was also bruising on
the same foot.  The employee did not require hospitalization.
At 11:18 a.m. on January 25, 2021, an employee worked to install an HVAC unit.
At some point, the employee fell approximately twenty feet and was killed due to
a head injury.
At 2:47 a.m. on January 22, 2021, an employee who worked  was an Office
Technician for a State contractor licensing board died from COVID-19 related
pneumonia.  The employee had primarily teleworked from home.  December 10, 2020,
was the last day she was physically in the office. On December 26, 2020, the
employee had reported COVID-19 related symptoms and she was tested on December
29, 2020. On December 30, 2020, the employee received a positive test result and
she was hospitalized on December 31, 2020. According to thye employee's family
member, she was treated in the emergency room on December 23, 2020, due to a
non-worked related health issue. At 5:40 p.m. on Monday, December 28, 2020, she
had stated "If I do come back positive the doctor said it probably came for me
going to the emergency room because I was perfectly fine other than my normal
issues I was having with my muscle atrophy so he thinks if I am positive it came
from there." (Her comments were entered into the narrative exactly as she had
sent it). The employer conducted contact tracing and did not identify any
COVID-19 positive coworkers.
An employee was working as a physician in a veteran's administration hospital
when she developed COVID-19 symptoms on November 9, tested positive on November
11, and subsequently died due to her infection on December 23, 2020.
At 10:00 p.m. on January 26, 2021, an employee who worked as a private sector
vocational trainer at a State mental facility died from COVID-19 infection. The
employee had been performing his regular duties at the facility
teaching/directing adults with mental and physical disabilities. On January 6,
2021, the employee was not showing symptoms but tested positive for COVID-19.

they were all from different departments having no interaction with each other.
An employee worked in administration for a public school district. The majority
of school operations have been conducted with employees working remotely from
home since the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic. The employee had been packing
gift baskets filled with sanitation supplies to be delivered to parents and
students. The employee was working alongside four coworkers. All were wearing
face masks but no plastic barriers were installed. The employer assumed they

operated the press for some four hours per day, two days per month. In this
incident, he was operating the press to punch holes in an aluminum extruded
part. The part was 3/16 in. (0.1875 in. or 4.78 mm) thick. The employee reached
into the point of operation to correct the orientation of the part in the
spanking die. At the same time, he inadvertently actuated the press by stepping
on the foot treadle. The index finger on his left hand was caught and crushed
where the top platen met the top of the return spring assembly on top of the
spanking die. His left index finger was amputated at its distal phalanx,
possibly surgically. He was treated without hospitalization. The point of
operation guards did not prevent the entry of hands or fingers into the press's
point of operation. The adjustable front point of operation guard was adjusted
so there was an approximately 2-in. (50-mm) gap between the bottom of the guard
and the top of the bolster plate. The adjustable guard was held in place by hex
socket cap screws. The press was set up to run in a manual operation and was
actuated by a foot switch. The press was fitted with a spanking die designed to
punch holes in the aluminum extruded part. An employee was able to reach under
the guard when he tried to reposition the aluminum extruded part in the spanking
die. The employee had been trained on how to operate the press and how to punch
holes in the aluminum extruded part. The hazard was in plain view of the
facility's maintenance and safety manager, who worked at the facility. He was
trained in machine guarding and was aware of the OSHA requirements for
mechanical power press guarding.

At approximately 9:00 a.m. on April 20, 2020, an employee was working at the

At 9:00 a.m. on April 7, 2021, Employee #1 was working from a Werner aluminum

At 8:00 a.m. on April 14, 2021, an employee, a maintenance technician, was

become energized. The electricity traveled from the receptacle through the
receptacle grounding conductor to the grounding lug terminal of the electrical
cabinet. The branch circuit and cabinet did not have a grounding conductor or
other grounding connection so the electricity energized the entire metal
electrical cabinet. The circuit had 150 amp fuses installed so they did not
interrupt the current when the electrical short occurred. The employee was
standing at the electrical cabinet in an area of the floor that was wet and was
electrocuted when he contacted the electrical cabinet. The employee was
transported to the hospital and died two days later.

At 3:00 p.m. on February 4, 2021, an employee was making one-pound tubes of

employee's middle and ring fingers on the right hand and resulted in partial

At 10:00 p.m. on January 19, 2021, Employee #1, a forklift operator, was on the

An employee was working as a used car manager in a car dealership where he

At 12:30 p.m. on April 27, 2021, an employee working as an electrician for a

pulled into the rollers, and Employee #1's right arm was pulled into the

At 07:45 a.m. on July 22, 2020, an employee was cutting plywood on a table saw.

The Division was notified on March 31, 2021, and arrived on site on April 6,

At 10:30 a.m. on December 14, 2020, Employee #1, a pipe layer, was spotting for

At 2:00 p.m. on March 29, 2021, an employee was operating a battery powered

An employee was working in a residential facility for individuals with

At 2:13 p.m. on March 9, 2021, an employee was riding a pallet jack. The

At 3:00 p.m. on April 15, 2021, an employee, a Survey Technician, was performing

by emergency medical services, hospitalized, and later died due to injuries of

At 7:15 a.m. on November 4, 2020, an employee was working for a firm that made
specialty frozen foods. She was a lead or line operator at a food processing
facility. She was inspecting equipment on line 6 after it had gone through
sanitation. Operators sanitized the line a minimum of every 44 hours of
production, per USDA/FDA regulations. The equipment was locked out during
sanitation but turned on and running during inspection. Operators had to see if
there were any food in the equipment before using it in production. The employee
was inspecting a "cluster buster." The cluster buster, located beneath a hopper,
had rotating paddles that broke up clumps of frozen vegetables. The employee was
using a 3- to 4-foot (0.9- to 1.2-m) ladder to inspect the cluster buster.
During sanitation, the cluster buster was positioned with an opening at the
bottom exposing its rotating parts. The cluster buster's opening for visual
inspection was 104 inches (8.66 feet, or 2.64 m) above the floor. It was 6.5
inches (165 mm) wide and 32 inches (0.81 m) long. While looking through the
opening with a flashlight to inspect the equipment, the employee noticed a piece
of carrot on one of the cluster buster's rotating paddles. She tried to dislodge
the piece of food from the rotating blade with a water hose for about ten
minutes. That didn't work. After several minutes of spraying with the water
hose, she gave up and reached into the rotating parts to clear the food with her
hand. The tip of the middle finger on her right hand was caught between a
rotating paddle and a fixed object. The tip of that finger was amputated. The
employee was treated without hospitalization. In an interview, the employee said
that the sanitation supervisor showed her how to use a stepladder to inspect and
wash away food in the cluster buster. The employee had been using the stepladder
for about two weeks before the incident. She said that she had not received
energy control training on line 6 before the incident.

While the employee was unhitching the vibrator, the operator of the excavator

At 11:00 a.m. on June 30, 2020, an employee was working in the warehouse area.

At 4:00 p.m. on October 5, 2020, an employee was operating a Cut System USA 3200

cut across the top of all five fingers of his right hand.  All five fingers on
the employee's right hand suffered deep lacerations with an amputation of two
fingers.

At 2:30 p.m. on November 1, 2020, an employee was attempting to connect two

At 12:00 p.m. on June 5, 2021, Employee #1 was stepping from the ground onto a

At 2:00 p.m. on Thursday, March 18, 2021, an employee was working for a firm
that manufactured gypsum products. He was on the second floor of the firm's
building. A scheduled shutdown had ended, and he was resuming work. He worked
with gypsum pieces that were moved on a GRT Rubber Technologies Accuform forming
board conveyor belt, with serial number 200000488. It was powered by a 480-volt
motor. There was a gap of 3 in. (76 mm) between the rollers where one section of
belt ended, and another section began. The end of each belt was about 36 in.
(0.9 m) above the floor. The belts traveled at 135 feet (41 m) per minute. The
diameter of the rollers was 3 in. (76 mm). The belts let gypsum boards lie flat
as they cured along the length of the belts. There was an unguarded nip point in
the gap between the rollers at the ends of the two belts. In this incident, the
employee put his hand in the nip point. His arm became lodged up to a point
above the elbow. He suffered severe skin abrasion causing first- and
second-degree burns. Some skin was removed. He was hospitalized. The apparatus
had been in the same approximate location and employees had been working on it
for at least a year. The hazard of unguarded rotating parts on the conveyor belt
had existed for approximately one year, exposing employees to injury. Employees'
hands, clothes, or tools could inadvertently reach the belts. Fixed guarding
would have inhibited employees from being injured. Each conveyor belt was wide
open and could easily be accessed from any location along the belt. The
employees operating the conveyor belts were required to work near the conveyor
belts, 1 foot (0.3 m) from the belts, for some one to four hours daily, placing
employees at the point of danger. At the time the investigator was conducting
the inspection, the employer was constructing guarding on conveyors to protect
employees from rotating parts in between conveyor belts. The employer had welded
guards to the belts' frames.

At 6:00 p.m. on June 11, 2021, an employee loaded a roller truck onto a

applied with the employee in the basket. The employee and scissor lift hit the

At 2:00 p.m. on February 24, 2021, an employee was attempting to help clear a

At 9:35 a.m. on February 22, 2021, an employee was working on changing the cups

At approximately 3:13 p.m. on May 28, 2021, an employee was working in a

At 11:45 a.m. on January 2, 2021, an employee who performed maintenance duties

At 9:00 a.m. on November 20, 2020, an employee working as a construction laborer

vertebrate.
At approximately 9:45 a.m. on May 28, 2021, an employee was operating a John

At 7:00 a.m. on December 14, 2020, Employee #1 was attempting to clear a piece

At 1:30 p.m. on February 14, 2021, an employee working as an automotive mechanic

employed by a steel erection company, and a jobsite coworker who was operating a
crane, were engaged in steel erection during construction of a new two-story
commercial building.  Employee #1 was preparing to connect one end of a rod -
which would act as a diagonal brace - to the bottom corner of the two-story
metal frame.  The rod was suspended from the crane's cable.  The crane operator
inadvertently came into contact with the crane controls, and the cable and
attached rod were jerked upward.  Employee #1 was pinned between the rod and the
metal frame/column he was leaning against.  Employee #1 sustained blunt force
traumatic crushing injuries and was killed.
At 2:00 p.m. on April 5, 2021, an employee was engaged in elevator installation
work. While exiting the elevator pit, the employee's finger got caught in the
moving equipment overhead. The employee was hospitalized and treated for an
amputation of the finger.
At 10:40 p.m. on July 20, 2021, an employee was hand cleaning a proofer infeed
belt when a coworker started the machine. The employee's right arm was pulled
into the machine rollers and he was crushed. Emergency services were notified
and the local fire department arrived and cut the conveyor belt to free the
employee. Paramedics transported the employee to a local hospital, where he was
pronounced dead.
At 3:30 p.m. on July 20, 2021, an employee, near the end of a 9-hour shift, was
setting a choker on a large white fir to be yarded up the corridor. Temperatures
were at or near 100 degrees Fahrenheit and the employees were likely fatigued.
The employee and a coworker began to move two trees with the motorized carriage
up the skyline. They were standing approximately 15 to 20 feet from the skyline
and logs to be skidded when the larger of the trees struck its stump causing it
to swing out and strike the employee in the chest.  The employee died from his
amputations to his middle and ring fingertips.
An employee was working as a telephone operator for a general medical and
surgical hospital. She worked at a corporate facility. She and her coworkers
worked in a room that was approximately 16 by 32 feet (4.9 by 7.3 meters) in
size. Employees worked in cubicles with sides and did not work face to face. The
employee began experiencing symptoms of illness on July 22, 2021. She received a
positive COVID-19 test on July 25, 2021. She died on August 2, 2021, of
respiratory issues due to COVID-19. Investigation 137803 covered the death of
her coworker. The coworker reported experiencing symptoms of COVID-19 on
approximately July 16, 2021. She was hospitalized on July 22, 2021. She died on
August 1, 2021, from respiratory issues due to COVID-19.
At 11:00 a.m. on July 22, 2021, Employee #1 was attempting to clear a board
jammed inside Planer #1 at a wood products facility. Before the machine came to
a complete stop, the employee reached his hand into the planer, where it was
armed with a knife. When officers arrived on scene, they located the employee
who had been critically injured in an attack. Police, firefighters and EMS
attempted to revive the employee, but she was pronounced dead at the scene.
Police arrested the suspect shortly after the incident. The employee had
previous problems with the suspect.
At 12:00 noon on August 27, 2021, an employee entered a tanker trailer to power
wash the interior of the tanker. The tanker had contained animal parts, and was
sitting outside in the high summer temperatures. The employee was found
unconscious inside the tanker and emergency services were notified. Upon
arrival, the fire department detected hydrogen sulfide at twice the level
considered to be immediately dangerous to life and health at the open manway on
the top of the tanker. No air monitoring had been done prior to entry into the
tanker. No attendant was in place and there was no retrieval system set up to
enable non-entry recue of the employee from outside the tanker. The employee
died due to asphyxiation.
An employee was working as an instructional assistant when she contracted
COVID-19 and subsequently died from her infection on August 29, 2021.
At 8:30 a.m. on August 26, 2021, two employees who both had been providing home
healthcare to COVID-19 positive residents were reported hospitalized due to
complications from contracting COVID-19. The date, time and other details
leading up to exposure are not indicated in the narrative. Information regarding
engineering, administrative and personal protective equipment controls for
COVID-19 are also not included in the narrative.
At 1:00 p.m. on July 10, 2021, an employee working as a cook in a full service
restaurant kitchen was cutting carrots with a knife. The employee lacerated his
finger and received medical treatment without hospitalization for an avulsion.
At 8:00 a.m. on September 1, 2021, Employee #1 was working as a mechanic,
assisting a driver in repairing the lights on the driver's tractor trailer. Once
Employee #1 had replaced some of the parts on the trailer, he went into the
garage, where everyone thought he was going to report to the garage supervisor
to discuss the day's activities.  Unbeknownst to the driver, Employee #1 then
came back out of the garage and walked to the back of the trailer to start
working on a brake light on the trailer.  The driver, not knowing that the
mechanic was back there, then began backing away from the building and ran over
the mechanic. Employee #1 was crushed under the wheels of the tractor trailer.
An employee was working as a principal lead hardware board design engineer for a
manufacturer of telecommunications equipment when he traveled to the company
headquarters for mandatory training in preparation for the launch of a new
product line. The employee attended the training sessions for two days until he
became ill and called his supervisor from the hotel early in the morning of the
third day and reported that he was sick with a runny nose, sore throat, and
symptoms of a bad cold. The employee stated that he did not think it was the
flu, much less COVID-19, because he was vaccinated. The employee did not report
to the training on the last day and flew back to the airport closest to his home
on July 16, 2021, arriving after midnight on July 17, 2021. The employee stayed
at a hotel close to the airport and then drove home later in the day. After
arriving home, the employee was transported by his daughter to the emergency
room at a local medical center, where he was admitted, tested positive for the
COVID-19 delta variant on July 18, 2021. The employee was placed on a ventilator
on July 20, 2021 and died on July 25, 2021 due to complications of COVID-19.
At 2:00 p.m. on August 26, 2021, an employee working for a materials recycler
was working on the outside grounds. The employee was attempting to adjust a
bearing on the head pulley of a conveyor belt. The employee was using a
come-a-long tool to remove the housing to access the bearing. The come-a-long
shifted as the employee was manually trying to remove the housing. The employee
caught his fingers between the housing and the frame of a conveyor gear box. The
employee was hospitalized  to treat amputations to both fingers and a crush
injury to another finger.
An employee was working as a home healthcare provider for her mother when she
contracted COIVD-19. The employee died from complications of her infection at
11:30 a.m. on August 30, 2021.
At 3:00 p.m. on August 30, 2021, an employee was trying to clear a jam of
product.  The employee was caught in the auger and was killed.
At 12:00 p.m. on August 31, 2021, an employee working for a metal products
manufacturer was moving a table saw guard down into position. His glove caught
on the sawblade. The employee was hospitalized to treat an amputation to his
finger.
At 9:00 a.m. on April 8, 2020, an employee who worked in an unspecified capacity
for a general medical and surgical hospital died from COVID-19.  The date, time
and other details leading up to exposure are not indicated in the narrative.

contacted emergency services and and when they arrived they pronounced the
employee dead.
At 5:30 a.m. on June 4, 2021, Employee #1 was operating an edger when the
machine became jammed. He lifted the hatch covering the sawing area to manually
clear the obstruction. While reaching into the equipment, his right hand made
contact with a saw blade, resulting in a partial amputation of his right index
finger. The employee was hospitalized for treatment.
At approximately 12:00 p.m. on July 5, 2021, an employee was quarantined due to
COVID-19 exposure. Employee tested positive for COVID-19 on July 12, 2021.  The
employer was contacted on July 24, 2021, with a notice that the employee died
from severe symptoms from COVID-19.
At 9:15 p.m. on February 24, 2021, an employee was performing a casing operation
on a drilling rig.  The air pressure released in a two-inch line, resulted in a
ball valve separating and striking the employee. The employee was hospitalized
to treat a fracture to the cheek bone.
At 12:08 p.m. on June 28, 2021, Employee #1 was driving a rear-loader garbage
truck downhill on a weekly residential route in Berkeley. The employee, acting
as a helper, was standing on the step located on the rear right side of the
truck. After the truck turned a corner and was traveling to the next house, the
employee stepped back onto the step. Simultaneously, a large tree limb fell from
residential property, striking the back of the truck and the employee. The
employee was knocked off the step and pinned to the ground. He sustained
multiple vertebrae and rib fractures and was admitted to Alameda Health System
Highland Hospital, where he underwent surgery the following day. The Division
found no violations related to the incident.
At 1:26 p.m. on May 2, 2021, an employee working at a car wash was precleaning a
car prior to running it through the automatic wash. When the car entered the car
wash, it pinned the employee between the car and another car being staged. The
employee was hospitalized to treat an amputated leg.
At 12:45 p.m. on July 20, 2021, Employee #1 was operating a hoist to lift a
ladle of molten iron when the ladle shifted, spilling molten iron onto the floor
and onto his right side. Employee #1 sustained third-degree burns to his right
leg and was hospitalized for treatment.
At 4:30 p.m. on September 30, 2020, an employee working for a global package
delivery company was operating a delivery truck delivering packages. The
employee began feeling dizzy and began to have trouble with his vision. The
ambient temperature at the time reached 109 degrees Fahrenheit. The employee
traveled to a nearby park (Yorba Linda) and a coworker (his supervisor) for
assistance. The employee waited in a naturally shaded area for assistance to
arrive. There was a local heat wave in the area at the time. The employee
received medical treatment for heat exhaustion but was not hospitalized.
At 7:00 a.m. on July 15, 2021, Employee #1 was riding on the back of a Tiger Cat
skidder while a coworker drove the machine into the woods to begin work. The
employee lost his balance and fell off the skidder, and the tires ran over his
legs. Emergency services transported Employee #1 to the hospital, where he was
admitted and treated for a broken left femur and a possible fracture to the
right hip.
At 6:00 a.m. on March 17, 2021, Employee #1 was working as a kitchen helper at a
grocery store and was operating a Hobart mixer. The employee was preparing to
use the Hobart to cut carrots when they noticed leftover cabbage bits in the
pelican head attachment. The employee turned off the Hobart to remove the debris
with their hand but became distracted and looked away. At the same time, the
employee placed his hand into the pelican head, where the finger was cut by the
still-rotating blade. There was one other employee present in the back kitchen,
but the employee was facing away from Employee #1. The supervisor was in the
front kitchen at the time of the accident. The employee suffered a laceration
and open fracture to the left-hand ring finger, requiring hospitalization for
three nights. Cal/OSHA identified two contributing factors: failure to clean the
pelican head attachment after prior use, and the employee's distraction while
handling the machine.
At 12:30 p.m. on June 3, 2021, Employee #1 was standing and talking with a

At 8:00 a.m. on Decembre 6, 2020, an employee who worked as a Licensed Practical

At approximately 12:00 p.m. on January 8, 2021, an employee was working as a

At 11:15 a.m. on January 7, 2021, an employee was on the loading dock picking up
packages when he was struck by semi-tractor-trailer truck backing into the
loading dock. The employee was pinned between the truck trailer and the loading
dock and was killed.
On September 8, 2020, an employee who performed maintenance duties at a food
manufacturing facility was hospitalized with COVID-19. The employee last worked
on September 1, 2020. The employee was tested and treated for COVID-19 before
being discharged on September 17, 2020. The company was found to have a robust
COVID-19 Tracking Program. The company had instituted a "quadrant check" which
required that employees sign-in and out from each quadrant of the plant in order
to track COVID-19 transmission by location. But, the date, time and other
details leading up to exposure are not indicated in the narrative.  Information
regarding engineering, administrative and personal protective equipment controls
for COVID-19 are not included in the narrative.
At 7:40 p.m. on December 14, 2020, Employee #1 was working on the 5/8 process
line at the Midlothian glass recycling plant. While addressing a conveyor belt
issue, the employee's jacket became caught in an adjacent conveyor, which
resulted in his right arm being crushed. Although the injury occurred without
witnesses, another employee reported that the employee had initially indicated a
problem with the conveyor line. Following the incident, the employee managed to
free himself and sought assistance from coworkers. After receiving first aid,
the employee was transported by company truck to Baylor Medical Center in
Waxahachie, TX, where he was admitted and underwent surgery for a broken forearm
between 2-3 a.m. As of the time of this report, the employee was still
hospitalized for observation.
At 10:00 a.m. on October 28, 2020, an employee working for a roofing and
insulation contractor was climbing an extension ladder. The ladder kicked out
from underneath the employee and he fell backwards off the ladder to the
concrete floor. The employee fractured his back and was hospitalized.
On July 6, 2020, an employee who had been a restaurant worker for a fast food
chain died from COVID-19. The employer could not determined the source of the
employee's exposure. The employer did not have Adequate Aerosol Transmissible
Diseases policies and procedures in place.
At 7:55 p.m. on January 6, 2021, Employee #1 was using a flashlight to inspect
inside a food wrapping machine. While doing so, the employee's finger was caught
in the machine's belt and pulley. As a result, the employee suffered an
amputation of the fingertip. The employee was treated without hospitalization.
An employee worked as a receiving clerk at a moving company.  The employee's
last day of work was December 4, 2020. The employee tested positive for the
COVID-19 virus on December 10, 2020. The employee was hospitalized for COVID-19
infection on December 13, 2020.  At 12:30   a.m. on January 1, 2021, the
employee died.
At approximately 3:05 p.m. on January 8, 2021, an employee was doing office and
managerial duties as the business manager.  The employee contracted COVID-19 and
later died from COVID-19 complications.
At approximately 4:00 p.m. on December 29, 2020, an employee was working as a
cashier. Someone came into the facility and jumped over the plexiglass barriers
and stabbed the employee to death with a knife.
At approximately 7:00 a.m. on January 6, 2021, an employee tested positive for
COVID-19 and later died from its complications.
At 1:30 p.m. on July 3, 2020, an employee (an indepenant contractor) was working
on an extension ladder installing a billboard sign at a strip mall  when he fell
approximately 15 feet to the concrete below. The employee required medical
treatment after hitting his head on the ground. The employee was not
hospitalized.
At 10:30 a.m. on January 8, 2021, Employee #1, a project manager for a painting
contractor, was working at a two-story residence.  He was climbing a 24-foot
extension ladder to access the roof when he reached out, causing the ladder to
slip and fall.  The employee fell and struck his head.  He was transported to
the hospital, admitted, and treated for a head injury.
At approximately 4:30 p.m. on December 3, 2020, an employee was climbing a
ladder to access an HVAC unit. The ladder utilized was incomplete, with half of
the extension missing, and it lacked safety feet, which posed a significant
safety hazard. The employee fell while using the ladder on a concrete floor,
resulting in a brain bleed that required surgical intervention and subsequent
memory loss.  The employee was hospitalized.
At 1:00 p.m. on November 15, 2020, an employee who worked as a Carpenter for a
construction company died from COVID-19. The employee was having difficulty
fill with steam.  Both employees could not open the door to exit due to the
pressurized steam.  Employee #1 was killed.
At 1:38 p.m. on November 17, 2020, Employee #1 and a coworker were engaged in a
street repaving.  Employee #1 was walking a pavement compactor from one location
along the street to another.  The coworker was operating a Peterbilt Material
Hauling Vehicle, Model 3-220.  As the coworker backed up the truck, the truck
ran over Employee #1.  Employee #1 sustained blunt force traumatic injuries and
was killed.
An employee was working as an MDS coordinator at a nursing care or skilled
nursing facility. An MDS coordinator is someone who assesses patients and
collects data for the minimum data set. Typically, an MDS coordinator is a
registered nurse (RN). She was performing her normal job duties, coding
residents' charts. On or about October 16, 2020, she tested positive for
COVID-19. She was hospitalized on or about October 25, 2020. She remained in the
hospital until she died there on or about November 13, 2020. She died due to
complications of COVID-19.
At 6:45 a.m. on November 9, 2020, an employee was loading an aerial work
platform into a box truck/liftgate. The aerial work platform tipped over and
fell, striking the employee's leg.  The employee was hospitalized to treat a
broken femur/leg.
At 3:00 a.m. on November 14, 2020, an employee, a master technician, was
troubleshooting a change over on a molding machine. The employee was
troubleshooting the molding machine, when there was an explosion. The employee
suffered second and third degree burns to the face from the molten plastic.  The
employee was hospitalized.
Four employees were working for a poultry hatchery. Employee #1 worked as a
general office clerk. She worked as a bookkeeping, auditing, or general
accounting clerk. She contracted COVID-19 and was admitted to a hospital on
February 13, 2021. She was hospitalized just before midnight, and she was
released the following day, February 14, 2021, just after noon. She was
hospitalized for twelve and a half hours, less than 24 hours. She reported to
her employer that she was infected by her daughter. This incident was not
work-related and thus not reportable. Employee #2 worked night shift as a
general laborer in the palletizing area. He worked alone much of the time or
with a limited night crew. He had limited contact with others on his shift. He
became ill with COVID-19 on November 23, 2020, and he was admitted to the
hospital that same day. It was also his last day of work. He was hospitalized
from November 23, 2020, through November 23, 2020, four days. He believed he
contacted COVID-19 at work, but he had no evidence of this. He stated that he
didn't know for sure how he got it. As of March 2021, he was still out from work
because of complications due to diabetes. Employee #3 worked as a general
laborer on the cook side in packaging. On September 2, 2020, she felt ill at
work and went home feeling bad. She was cold, and her bones ached. She left work
at her normal time. The following day, she called her employer, who told her to
get tested for COVID-19. The test came back positive on September 4, 2020, and
she was hospitalized that same day. She was not sure how she was infected, but
she denied getting COVID-19 from a family member. She said that she was
hospitalized for ten days, but the hospital records showed a hospitalization of
four days. She said that she was on oxygen for two months and off work for three
months. Employee #4 worked as a laborer. He was hospitalized, but there was no
further information provided about him.

All four employees were hospitalized due to contracting  COVID-19.  The

Employee #3 started not feeling well and was tested for COVID-19 on February 13,

At 4:30 p.m. on August 26, 2020, an employee was nailing wood framing at the
edge of the second level floor at approximately 12.2 feet from the ground, when
he stepped on a 2 by 4 wood piece that tipped.  As he stepped onto the 2 by 4
that tipped, he fell off the edge of the building approximately 12.2 feet onto
the concrete floor.  He did not have fall protection.  He refused medical
treatment at the time of the accident; as it was the end of the day when the
accident occurred, he rested inside the structure and then went home.  The
employee reported to work the following day and complained of back pain.  He was
taken to Concentra Clinic, then transferred to Henry Mayo Newhall Hospital.  The
employee was noted to have lumbar transverse process fractures with associated
retroperitoneal hematoma. The employee was admitted to the hospital with no
surgery recommended and was ordered physical therapy.  He was discharged on
August 28, 2020.
At 8:00 p.m. on January 18, 2021, an employee who worked as a Nursing Assistant
for a licensed skilled nursing facility was hospitalized with COVID-19
infection. The employee had been providing direct patient care to COVID-19
patients during the week of January 11, 2021. The employee did not respond to
multiple  requests for an interview, so some details leading up to the exposure
are not known. The employee had been required to wear a fit tested N95 as part
of the employer's respiratory protection program when working at the facility.
The employer conducted an exposure analysis and concluded there was no
definitive source of the exposure. Follow-up interviews and document review
indicated that the exposure analysis was flawed and was missing several required
elements. In addition, the employer did not have Adequate Aerosol Transmissible
Diseases policies and procedures in place.
An employee was working as an activities assistant in an assisted living
facility when she developed symptoms of COVID-19. The employee called in sick on

Inverter Generator. Employee #1 plugged his cellphone charger to the plugin
outlet of the Predator 2000 Inverter Generator to charge his cellphone at night.
The employee went to sleep with the generator running inside the trailer with
the windows closed. One window was cracked less than 2 inches open. The employee
was found by a coworker the next morning dead.  The generator had ran out of
fuel, stopped working when employee was found the next morning by a coworker.
Employee #1 was killed by asphyxiation due to carbon monoxide.
At 11:30 p.m. on March 6, 2021, an employee was loading a piece of lead into a
smelter when he fell into the smelter. The employee died from extreme burns.
At 11:30 p.m. on February 22, 2021, two employees, yard jockeys, were operating
tractors in the warehouse yard, when they collided. One of the employees was
hospitalized to treat fractured ribs and a collapsed lung.
At 8:00 a.m. on February 19, 2021, Employee #1 was working for a painting
contractor.  Employee #1 was walking down a flight of steel stairs that were
part of a scaffold stair tower system. Employee #1 slipped on the snow-covered
stairs.  Employee #1 suffered a back strain and lacerations. Employee #1 was
hospitalized.
At 10:00 a.m. on July 21, 2020, Employee #1, employed by a painting company, was
working at a residence.  He was working from a ladder jack scaffold with no
personal fall protection and scraping paint from the rear of the residence.  As
he reached out at the end of the scaffold, he lost his footing and fell, a fall
height of 12 feet.  The employee held onto his scraper as he fell.  When the
employee hit the ground, the scraper was in a straight up position.  Employee
#1's throat was impaled by the scraper.  The employee was killed.
At 9:30 a.m. on March 1, 2021, Employee #1 was loading and unloading a robotic
weld station when his left index finger was amputated. The employee was not
protected by a light curtain at the load/unload station of the pneumatic weld
fixture. Emergency services were contacted, and the employee was hospitalized
for treatment.
At 8:34 p.m. on November 5, 2020, Employee #1, employed by a general contracting
company specializing in waterproofing, was working at the top of the south
exterior wall preparing to set up a 40-foot long suspended power platform. While
attempting to straighten out a kink in the cable, the kink suddenly straightened
itself, pinching the employee's right hand. The middle, ring, and pinky fingers
were caught in the pinch, resulting in the amputation of the tip of the pinky
finger. The middle and ring fingers were re-attached, but the first digit of the
pinky could not be found. The employee was hospitalized for seven days for
treatment.
On December 15, 2020, three employees who worked in an office environment with
cubicles or in a warehouse packing items into boxes were reported hospitalized
with COVID-19. The employees were hospitalized between November 2020 and January
2021. The employer had policies to protect workers from contracting COVID-19
including mandatory mask wearing, social distancing rules, barriers, daily
temperature and symptom screening, frequent disinfection of surfaces, rules for
return to work following illness and contact tracing notifications for employees
potentially exposed to an infected coworker. One employee died from his illness
on January 21, 2021, due to related health issues and severe acute respiratory

At 3:15 p.m. on February 21, 2021, an employee was preparing to cut branches off
of a tree trunk (16 feet long, 12-18 inch diameter) held be a grappler rake
attachment on a Caterpillar 277b skid steer. The grappler did not have an
adequate grip on the tree trunk. The tree trunk rolled out of the grappler
attachment and struck the employee.  The employee was hospitalized to treat
multiple fractures to the body.
At 11:00 a.m. on January 28, 2021, Employee #1 was installing counters for a
restroom renovation in a 19-story commercial building.  He was using a pair of

lacerated.  The employee was transported to the hospital and admitted for

At 9:45 a.m. on August 22, 2020, an employee working as a machine operator for a

employee worked directly for the employer. The employee was working in the

the unguarded portion of a pinch point. The employee partially amputated a
finger, requiring medical treatment without hospitalization.
At 9:30 a.m. on November 25, 2020, an employee was moving a refrigerator with a

fractured hip.
At 1:30 p.m. on February 24, 2021, Employee #1 was walking alongside and in
front of a front-end loader while guiding a large palm tree that was suspended
by the loader's boom. The employee lost his balance and slipped, causing his
right leg and ankle to be run over and crushed by the front wheel of the
front-end loader. The employee sustained fractures to his right leg and ankle.
He was transported to the hospital for admission and further care.
At 9:15 a.m. on January 1, 2021, Employee #1 walked into the break room to clock
in after a break, at a supermarket. Employee suddenly collapsed to the floor
from apparent cardiac arrest. Employee #1 was killed.
At 5:00 a.m. on February 5, 2020, Employee #1 was working for a site preparation
contractor.  Employee #1 was emptying bags of salt into the back of a truck.
Employee #1 shut the tailgate of the truck on his finger.  Employee #1 suffered
an avulsion of the finger. Employee #1 received medical treatment but was not
hospitalized.
An employee was working for a public transportation system when he was exposed
to passengers and coworkers infected with COVID-19. The employee contracted
COVID-19 and subsequently required hospitalization to treat his infection at
8:00 p.m. on November 23, 2020.
At 8:45 a.m. on March 3, 2021, an employee working as a truck driver for an
injury later required amputation by a doctor.
At 8:00 a.m. on December 30, 2019, an employee way placing lifting slings around
steel reinforcing bar (rebar) in preparation for hoisting. The employee was
working under a suspended load, when the load (5,500-pounds of rebar) fell onto
of him and pinned the employee to the flatbed trailer he was standing on. The
employee received fractures to multiple ribs and spine, internal injuries with
bleeding and was killed.
At 9:30 a.m. on December 3, 2020, an employee was working for a firm that
manufactured conveyors and conveying equipment. She was a temporary assembly
worker. The narrative did not say whether she had come from a temporary staffing
agency or had been reassigned from duty elsewhere in the firm. There was no
second UPA. The employee was operating a two-hand control swager or swaging
machine. It was a kind of hydraulic press. The employee would place a plastic
conveyor connector inside the metal tube. The machine would then crimp the metal
on either end of the tube to keep the plastic connector in place. The time, the
tube was pulled out of alignment. When the employee put the tube back into the
proper alignment within the tube clamp, her right middle finger was caught
inside the clamp and amputated. The employee was hospitalized. It was known that
the two-hand control device had never functioned properly. Three other employees
who all used the swager machine said during their interviews that when they
removed their hands from the two-hand control device, the swager would continue
to operate. Two of these employees explained that there wasn't any other
guarding, and that the two-hand control device never stopped the swager from
operating, even when they removed their hands from the two-hand control device.
The firm's chief financial officer said in an email that the firm had begun
using the swager in October 2020. The vice president of operations said during
his interview that he had worked on the swagger when it first arrived. When he
used the machine, it would continue to cycle, even when he removed his hands
from the control device. He added that there were no other guards. During the
walkaround, the CSHO was led to believe by the warehouse manager that the
control device had initially worked, but that it had malfunctioned. The employer
had put the machine into service knowing that it was not functioning correctly.
The employer explained that this was a new company.

their procedures for cleaning the fillers. They had maintenance install
individual disconnects that could be locked out next to each of the fillers.
They also developed LOTO procedures for the fillers and trained employees on
them. This incident had inspection number 1516267.
